cities.d: the capital of Turkey and its second largest city

x.around: The city has a dense bus network, a two-line Metro, and an east-west suburban railway called Başkentray. There is no provision by any mode of public transport for travellers with restricted mobility. EGO (or toplu taşıma) is the municipality public transportation company.

hidden.d: Contemporary art museum in the former power plant for Turkish Railways.
A collection of two dozen military aircraft.
More chess sets ancient and modern than you'd think possible, including weird versions such as the three-sided game.
Extensive display of Turkish painters and artists from the early days of the Republic until present times.
A prehistoric cave, extensively decorated, discovered during construction of the ring road.
Built by the famous architect Sinan in 1566, it's in finely-crafted Ankara stone. The mimber (pulpit) and mihrap (prayer niche) are of white marble.

x.intro: Ankara is the capital of Turkey, central within the country on the plateau of Central Anatolia. It's a sprawling modern place around an ancient citadel, and in 2022 had a population of almost 5.2 million (second in size to Istanbul), with a further 600,000 living in the wider metropolis.

must.d: Excellent display ranging from prehistory to the proto-Greek and Roman eras.

n.es: Museo de las Civilizaciones de Anatolia

must.d: This had been in the planning since 1944, but attempts at a modern style were thwarted by the conservatives. So what was built from 1967 to 1987 is a neoclassical Ottoman structure.

This volcanic outcrop has probably been fortified since the dawn of mankind, but the earliest traces are from the Phrygians of 8th century BC. The castle was reinforced by the Galatians then the Romans.

Built in 1290 in Seljuk style, and repaired in 1330 under Ahi Şerafeddin hence its other name. Well worth the hike up the hill for its finely-carved interior, notably the ceiling supported by a forest of wooden columns.
Built from 1927, this hosts a permanent display of Turkish art from late 1800s to present day, plus temporary exhibitions.

This was built in 1428, restored by Mimar Sinan in the 16th century, and with Kütahya tiles added in the 18th. Hacı Bayram Veli (1352–1430) was a poet and Sufi teacher, and his ornate tomb is a pilgrimage site.

Ruins of a large Roman bath complex, built under Emperor Caracalla circa 200 AD and in use for 500 years. They follow the classical design of frigidarium (cold room), tepidarium (warm room) and caldarium (hot room), and their…
Large museum of science and technology. Has a particularly good collection of military aircraft, and a large steam locomotive.

next.d: Çayırhan and Nallıhan.
northeast is the hub for visiting ancient Hattuşa, the capital of Hittites.
("Salt Lake") on the road to Aksaray.
off the highway to Eskişehir. One of the most important ancient cities in Turkey, it had been home for Hittites, Phyrigians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans since 3000 BC.

x.safe: Ankara is generally safe, even for single females at night, since as the capital it's well-policed. (The cops are looking for traffic offences, dissident trouble-makers and squaddies in town without a liberty pass.) Take usual care of valuables. The main hazard is traffic - vehicles are driven at silly speeds with scant regard to traffic lights and pedestrians.

cities.d: the fastest growing city, hub to an array of beach resorts

x.around: In addition, Antalyakart is the plastic transport card you may use to get additional benefits. Buy it or reload it at kiosks along the tramway, at the airport and at the bus terminal; you probably need banknotes for this.

hidden.d: Sand sculpture park open year round, lit up at night.
Atatürk stayed in Antalya in 1930, 1931 and 1935. This rebuilt mansion shows memorabilia of his times.
Large spacious zoo park.

Sea lions and dolphins do their splashy stuff at 11:00 and 15:00. Extra charges to swim with them or have a dolphin take a photo of you. People may wish to consider the ethics of such attractions before visiting.
An attractive pool in a canyon.

A hilltop of 618 m with great views over the city and coast, reached by gondola cable car though you can drive or even hike up. Food and drink at the top station are a silly price. The cable car collapsed in April 2024.
Huge aquarium with display tanks and long viewing tunnel.

x.intro: Not to be confused with Alanya, a resort 130 km further east, or with Antakya a historic city in Hatay province of eastern Turkey. Antalya is a city in Pamphylia on the Turkish Mediterranean coast, and the chief resort of the "Turkish Riviera". It's a metropolis with a population of 2.7 million in 2022, the fifth largest city in the country.

must.d: Extensive ruins of a city which had its heyday 2nd to 3rd century AD under the Romans. The site has a colonnaded agora, theatre, stadium, temple to Artemis and two churches.

Graeco-Roman city, of which the centrepiece is the well-preserved amphitheatre, seating 7000. There's also 2 km of aqueduct (which siphoned water over rises), a stadium, baths, basilica, agora and nymphaeum.
Elegant six-domed mosque built under Seljuk rule in 1230 and rebuilt in 1373 by the Hamidids. The minaret is 38 m tall.
One of Turkey's largest museums, with 5000 items illustrating the history of the Mediterranean and Pamphylia regions. It's also a repository for some 25,000 items not on display.

Built by the Romans in the 2nd century AD with a square base and circular upper storey, this was a bastion and lighthouse. Its present name indicates that it's the site of Hıdırellez on 5/6 May, a religious spring festival.
This was first built as a Roman temple in the 2nd century AD, and in later centuries went back and forth between religions.

Woodland park, the waterfalls are impressive in flow but dry to a trickle in summer. A firm path leads you past the best views but is not suitable with restricted mobility. There are refreshment stalls and a café/restaurant.

next.d: southwest is part of the Antalya tourist strip. Go further south along the rugged coast of Lycia for quiet beaches and village harbours.
to the east has golf links and luxury hotels.
further east has waterfalls, but the big draw is the Roman ruins at Side.
yet further east has an ancient citadel perched on a crag, with beach hotels stretching either side.
is a ruined ancient city above the forests of the Taurus Mountains.

x.safe: Standard precautions about traffic, water and sun safety, care of valuables and avoiding drunks.

cities.d: a trendy coastal town in Southern Aegean which turns into a crowded city in season when it serves as a playground for Turkish and international holidaymakers alike, featuring a citadel, Roman ruins,…

x.around: Most town buses start from Yeni Otogar the inter-city bus terminal and run to downtown Bodrum, so this service is every couple of minutes. They then fan out across the peninsula: * Bus 2-28 to Gümbet beach strip, Bitez, Müskebi, Ortakent and Camel Beach, every 20 min daily 07:00-00:00. * Bus 2-34 to Gürece, İslamhaneleri, Akçaalan and Turgutreis, every ten minutes daily 07:00-00:00.

hidden.d: A park with 23 waterslides, a 350-m wave river, a wave pool, a range of other pools, and a disco. Food is overpriced and they search you to keep it that way.
Zeki Müren (1931-96) was a prolific, flamboyant and frankly camp singer-songwriter. He was born in Bursa, launched his career in Istanbul and retired to Bodrum when his health failed.

x.intro: Bodrum is a tourist resort on the Southern Aegean coast of Turkey. It's a budget, mass-market destination with facilities to match, and in 2020 the Bodrum metropolis had a population of almost 182,000.

must.d: Mausolos was satrap (regional governor) here for 18 years. Before his death in 353 BC, he commissioned a tomb for himself so grand that it was accounted one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and "mausoleum" became the…

Well-preserved bastion built from 1402 by the Knights Hospitaller, who called it the Castle of St Peter. Its towers are called the English, French, German and Italian for the four nations constructing them, a clue as to why this…

n.en: Bodrum Castle / Museum of Underwater Archaeology
n.es: Castillo de San Pedro de Halicarnaso

must.d: This was begun by Mausolos in the 4th century BC, but took its present form under the Romans in the 2nd century AD. It was restored in the 1970s and 90s into an event space with seating for 10,000.

next.d: Gümüşlük and Yalıkavak.
is the Greek island 20 km southwest, often visited as a day-trip.
are three Greek ruins on the ridge 80 km north.
is a big resort town just beyond that ridge, with must-see Ephesus 20 km further inland.
is an unspoilt town to the south across the Gulf of Gökova, accessible by ferries or a long detour via Marmaris.

cities.d: the second capital of the Ottoman Empire

x.around: The centre is compact, fairly flat and walkable. The outlying districts are within a long walk, but you might prefer to take a taxi or dolmuş at least one way.

hidden.d: (Adalet Kasrı) by Fatih Bridge is a sturdy square tower, the last intact remnant of the palace.
The original museum from 1924 was part of the mosque complex; it moved here in 1971 as the collection expanded. The museum displays the area's eventful history, majoring on the Thracian period.
Monument to Rüştü Pasha, the commander defending the city during the Balkan Wars of 1913. The small museum adjacent is closed indefinitely "for restoration".
The 19th century house is a major Baha'i shrine; the religion's founder, Baháʼu'lláh, lived here for four years during his Ottoman exile.
on the island is an arena for oil-wrestling, with statues of past champions.
a historic stone bridge across the river Tunca
A vast hilltop redoubt and fortress built from 1829 against Russian attack, though its finest hour was in the Balkan Wars of 1913. It had little value against 20th century weaponry and fell derelict.

x.intro: Edirne (pronounced eh-deer-neh) is the chief city of Eastern Thrace, in the Marmara Region of northwest Turkey. It lies on the gently rolling Thracian plains at the confluence of three rivers, close to the borders with Greece and Bulgaria. Most visitors crossing those borders drive straight on east, or stay on the bus or train, to reach Istanbul.

must.d: Magnificent mosque that dominates the city skyline, approach from northwest to appreciate the full effect and miss the shops. It's the masterpiece of Mimar Sinan, built 1569-75, and listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
This was built in the 15th century, so it's the oldest and smallest of the city's three imperial mosques. It's a low building with nine domes and two minarets, with striking calligraphy within.
Mosque built 1438-1447, its name refers to the three balconies or galleries on its tallest minaret. The other three minarets are all of different designs.
The great fire of 1905 destroyed its predecessor, so this synagogue was opened in 1909 to serve the large Jewish population.
Bulgarian Orthodox church built in 1869.

n.en: Church of Sts. Constantine and Helen
n.it: chiesa dei Santi Costantino e Elena

must.d: This was built 1435 / 36 as part of a Mevlevi dervish complex but later became a stand-alone mosque. It has beautiful tile work, especially in the mihrab, probably by the "Masters of Tabriz" who decorated the mosque in Bursa and…
Bulgarian Orthodox church on a basilica pattern, opened in 1880 and still in use. Usually locked except for services but the caretaker might let you in.
This complex was founded by Sultan Bayezid II in 1484. As well as the hospital there was a medical school, mosque, guesthouse, almshouse and Turkish baths.

next.d: literally "the long bridge", has a remarkable 15th century stone bridge of 174 arches.
further south is just a transport hub, but you have to go that way to reach the beach resorts along the Gulf of Saros.
is the must-see metropolis to the southeast.

x.safe: Floods are a hazard after heavy rain especially in winter. Districts such as Karaağaç may be cut off as the medieval bridges become inundated. Never try to cross a flooded bridge, see local advice on work-around safe routes.

cities.d: Turkey's largest city, the former capital of both the Ottoman and Byzantine Empires, and the only major city in the world to straddle two continents

x.around: İETT (or just toplu taşıma) is the municipality's public transportation company. Istanbul's public transit system can be difficult to figure out. However, if you put some effort into it, you can avoid taxis and not walk too much.

hidden.d: This former synagogue of Ashkenazi Jews (many of German or French origin) now hosts an art gallery downstairs. Upstairs, there is an exhibition about the arrival and the lives of Ashkenazi Jews in Istanbul, with many original…
The Pelit company has made chocolate since 1957. This small museum is dedicated to the history of chocolate in Turkey and also features numerous chocolate sculptures.
Next to the Court of Istanbul.

A mostly upscale suburb on the coast of the Sea of Marmara, just south of the former airport. It was a multicultural village during the Ottoman period — the legacy of which still lives on in numerous churches of different…

Feshane began as a factory producing fezzes (fes), the red hats made of felt adopted by the Ottomans in the early 19th century as a part of westernizing efforts in lieu of much more traditional turbans.
A ritual dancing hall of the mystical Mevlevi order, the followers of the teachings of Mewlānā Rumi. The quiet and peaceful garden is a welcome escape from the hustle and bustle of Beyoğlu.

x.intro: Istanbul (Turkish: İstanbul) is a very large city of fantastic history, culture and beauty. Called Byzantium in ancient times, the city's name was changed to Constantinople in 324 CE when it was rebuilt by the first Christian Roman Emperor, Constantine. The name "Istanbul", perhaps surprisingly, comes from Greek and could be translated as a corruption of "to the city".

must.d: The third and grandest of the churches on this site, completed in 537 AD. The 30-m diameter dome covers what was for over 1000 years the largest enclosed space in the world, only surpassed in 1520 by Seville cathedral.

The defining image of Istanbul, dominating the skyline with its great dome and six minarets. Completed in 1617 for Sultan Ahmed I, it's still a working mosque, so dress appropriately and avoid prayer times.
The imperial enclave of the Ottoman emperors for four centuries. Lavishly decorated, with exhibitions of fine craftmanship and four courts of increasing grandeur.

On top of a hill overlooking the Golden Horn, this is a magnificent mosque built by Sinan in the 1550s. It was centrepiece of a large külliye, a religious complex which included madrasas, a public kitchen and a hospital..

This is modest from the outside, as the Ottomans would not permit non-Muslim religious buildings to rival the mosques. The interior is lavish but its chief importance is as the senior Eastern Orthodox church.
It was built by the Genoese in the 14th century on the city walls of Galata, marking the highest point of their territory.

This lavish palace with 285 rooms and 43 halls was the admin centre for the Ottoman Empire in its last 60 years. The palace government block (Selamlık) includes the Imperial Mabeyn (State Apartments) and Muayede Hall (Ceremonial…
Vast underground cistern built by Justinian in 532 to store the city's water, the largest and best-known of the hundreds constructed. It's a cathedral-like space with 336 richly decorated columns.

next.d: two hours to the northwest, is a beautiful historic city, and was the Ottoman capital before power moved to Istanbul. You need at least a day here.
in Bulgaria or Bucharest in Romania.
all the way to the Adriatic and across to Rome.
are across the sea, much further away and less urban than the Princes Islands just offshore of the city.
to the southeast is a former Ottoman capital with many historical sights plus Uludağ National Park just south.
is to head west then south into the Gallipoli peninsula, with its World War I sites, cross the Dardanelles to Çanakkale, then past ancient Troy and Pergamon (Bergama).

x.safe: Also be aware of friendly behaving groups of young men or male-female couples striking up a conversation in the street and inviting you to a "good nightclub they know". This has frequently been reported as a prelude to such a scam. The people in on the scam may offer to take you to dinner first, in order to lower your suspicions.

cities.d: Turkey's third largest city, hub to an array of beach resorts

x.around: İzmirim Kart is the contactless smart card used for all modes of public transport, available from multiple locations including the airport, ferry piers, and railway and metro stations. Each use is valid for 90 min, including one interchange on tram, train and metro but not buses. In 2024 a city centre bus journey costs 8.78 TL then a first transfer is 3.50 TL.

hidden.d: Ruins of the marketplace of Hellenistic and Roman Smyrna.
Large collection of antique cars and motorbikes.
Mostly Hellenistic statues, ceramics and coins.
The ruins of the very first Smyrna.
Former Greek Orthodox church, now used as a cultural centre.
Showing the days when public information was gathered by clustering around the radio.
Neo-classical mansion with rooms used by Atatürk.

x.intro: İzmir is a port on the Central Aegean coast of Turkey, known in antiquity as Smyrna. It's the country's third-largest city, with a population of 3.12 million in 2024.

must.d: This lift was constructed in 1907 by Nesim Levi Bayrakoğlu, a Jewish businessman, to carry people and goods between Karataş waterfront and the properties on the hill.
Around 330 BC during the reign of Alexander the Great, the population moved off the cramped site now known as "Old Smyrna", to fortify this hilltop.
Displays a large collection of finds from Smyrna and other Ionian cities, mostly Roman. There's also a numismatic section with ancient coins and jewellery.
Birdwatching park in the salt marshes of Gediz Delta, one of Turkey's largest coastal wetlands. It's partly artificial, as the Gediz was diverted here to reduce silting of the port.

next.d: is a small harbour half an hour's drive west of Izmir. It has ferries to Chios.
a few hours to the south has many historical sights, and is the hub for reaching the must-see Roman city of Ephesus.
is a pleasant inland village, renowned for its wines.
further east is one of the prettiest in the country.
northeast over Sabuncubeli Pass is the hub for visiting Sardes, the capital of ancient Lydia, and Mount Sipylus with forest scenery and mythological sites.
north has the ruins of Pergamon, among the top sights in the country.

x.safe: Usual care of valuables, and beware traffic. There's a police post on Konak Pier and the HQ - for something serious like a missing passport - is on 1365th Sk near Basmane Station. There's no longer a separate "tourism police".

cities.d: a quite large city that is the heartland of mystic Sufi order, the site of Rumi's tomb, and with some elegant Seljuq architecture, all surrounded by vast steppes

x.around: Trams run 06:00 to midnight. Line 1 runs north-south from Selçuk University via the bus terminal and Selçuklu YHT station to Zafer / Alaaddin Hill in city centre. Line 2 runs east-west from Alifbey via the Mevlana Cultural Centre and Mevlana Cd to Zafer / Alaadin Hill. They loop the hill then head back out.

hidden.d: Attractive display of finds from the region, especially the carved sarcophagi and discoveries at Çatalhöyük.
Modern science museum with hands-on exhibits and planetarium.

Sema is the authentic dervish ceremony, traditionally held in the Centre on Saturday at 19:00 winter, 20:00 summer. During the weeks culminating in the Şeb-i Arûs, "reunion night", commemorating Rumi's death on Dec 17, the…

x.intro: Konya is a city in Central Anatolia in Turkey, known as the city of "whirling dervishes" and for its outstanding Seljuk architecture. In 2021 Konya metropolis had a population of 2,277,017, the sixth largest in Turkey, but the area of most interest is compact.

must.d: Rumi (1207–1273) was a Persian poet, philosopher and teacher who lived in Konya after the Byzantine Romans had been ousted but the area was still known as "Rum".
Medrassa built in 1251 and now a museum of Seljuk tiles.

This medrassa (seminary) was built in 1265. Ince Minaret means "slender minaret" – it was originally taller, but a lightning blast in 1901 toppled it through the mosque dome; the re-build is distinctly stumpy.
This mosque was built in 1202 AD (598 AH), a brick Seljuk structure. İplikçi means "thread spinner" and İplikçi Necîbüddin Ayaz was a trustee of the adjacent madressa.

next.d: 1 hour's drive away from Konya, this archeologically hugely important prehistoric site is one of the earliest and most well preserved human settlements discovered.
A pretty little town in the northwest of Konya province, which was home of the Hoca, a Sufi sage famous for his folk wit. The city holds a Hoca festival in July.
A laid-back city and great hub for the surrounding attractions near Güzelyurt, or like Tuz Gölü ("Salt Lake"), the second largest lake in Turkey is becoming a popular day trip from the Cappadocian…
3 hours east is a must-see unworldly landscape.
Has a medieval centre. It's a stop-off on the way to Adana, and you change here for transport to the coast, for ferries to Cyprus.

cities.d: the wonderful Sumela Monastery is just outside the city and it is a great gateway to exploring the Turkish Northeast

x.around: "Take my camel, dear", said my Aunt Dot, as she climbed down from this animal on her return from High Mass. ::: - The Towers of Trebizond (1956) by Rose Macaulay follows a group of conflicted dingbats on a journey from Istanbul

hidden.d: Restored mansion with photographs, documents and artefacts describing the city in the Ottoman and Republican periods. Signage is only in Turkish.
Built in 1987 in retro style on the site of an earlier mosque.
Ottoman mosque built in 1789 around a pre-existing church.
Built in its present form in 1577, this is no longer in use, replaced by a larger modern mosque adjacent.
Majoring on space and aerospace, with planetarium. M-F it may be booked out to school groups.
Art space and cultural centre in the former city governor's mansion.
Former Greek Orthodox church founded in 1306 outside the city walls - exoteichos- but rebuilt in 1856 very much hemmed in by the city. It's now used as an annex to a primary school.

Founded in 1514 by Selim, then governor and later Sultan, in honour of his mother. Gulbahar Hatun (1453-1505) was originally a slave girl and became the concubine of Bayezid II; her tomb is here. The mosque was repaired in 1883.

x.intro: Trabzon is the largest city in the Eastern Karadeniz region of Turkey, with a population of 323,000 in 2023, and another 500,000 in the outlying towns. It was once known as Trebizond, ruling an independent "Empire" around the eastern Black Sea. It's now a lively place with good visitor facilities and attractions.

must.d: A spectacular monastery hewn into a cliff. It was founded in the fourth century, with its heyday in Byzantine and early Ottoman times. It's been ruined and rebuilt several times, but fell derelict after its Greeks were deported.

The city's top sight, a Byzantine church built in the 1250s, with beautiful frescoes, arches and friezes. It became a mosque in 2013 whereupon pre-Islamic features were covered up, but most of these were uncovered in 2020.

The "Golden domed church of All Saints" was built in the 10th or 11th century on much earlier foundations - until the 4th century AD it was the scene of Mithras worship.In the Middle ages it was the city cathedral, and hosted…
Built in the 13th century as a church dedicated to Saint Eugenius, the patron saint of the city. Eugenius was a martyr under the persecutions of Diocletian around 305 AD.

Dinky little Greek Orthodox basilica from 6th / 7th century AD, one of the oldest buildings in the city. It fell out of use when the Greeks were deported and many frescos were painted over, but in 2021 / 22 it was all restored.
Founded in 752 AD, Saint George Peristereota Monastery is now just a few walls teetering on a crag, with cliffs and other pitfalls around: don't come in the fog and drizzle.
The Armenian Monastery of the All-Saviour is on a hill southeast of town. Its foundation date was maybe 1424 AD, over an earlier Greek church.

Founded in 270 AD as one of the first-ever Christian monasteries, now ruined and unsafe. Take the road off D885 towards Köprüyanı, then the track branching uphill from the first hairpin bend - this is only suitable for…

next.d: is a small resort 18 km west.
west is a lively coast resort.
east has a few tourist attractions, but is mostly a stopover heading into the mountains or into Georgia.
is the first place you reach in Georgia. Trabzonites regard it as Las Vegas-on-Sea.
is a mountain resort above Trabzon.
south across Zigana Pass is a base for walking in the hills.
is the next city beyond the mountains.

x.safe: In the city beware traffic, safeguard valuables and avoid lowlife, same as anywhere else.

cities.d: a city with beautiful architecture and extremely friendly locals at the gates of Eastern World; where Turkish, Kurdish, Arabic, and Assyrian cultures mingle

x.around: The city has a network of minibus lines, although all sights are located in the easily walkable compact old town.

hidden.d: Extensive tombs that can be seen from the street.
Urfa is believed to have been the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham (İbrahim in Turkish and Arabic) and so is an important Islamic place of pilgrimage.

x.intro: Urfa (also Şanlıurfa, formerly Edessa) is a city in Southeastern Anatolia, and the provincial capital of Şanlıurfa Province. The city is about 80 km east of the Euphrates River, and with a population of 600 thousand is smaller than nearby Gaziantep.

must.d: If it is a temple, as some think, it is the oldest yet found in the world. Dated to 9000 BCE and listed by UNESCO as a world heritage site, Göbekli Tepe has changed the way that archaeologists look at history as it pre-dates…

The ancient ruined castle with newer walls dating from around 814 AD on the rocky promontory at the south side of town. A lone column is just about all that remains of the older structure but the views are spectacular.

next.d: about 200 km to the east, with its stonework architecture and Syriac Orthodox churches is another interesting place to visit in the region.
the mountain of gods, or Diyarbakır, the largest city of the region also full of history. Both are within a day's reach of Urfa.
is a riverside old town in the west, partially swallowed by a dam lake.

x.safe: Urfa seems to be a very safe city. There is a police sentry box in the Balıklıgöl/Pool area where you can report any problems.

intro: Turkey (Turkish: Türkiye), officially the Republic of Türkiye (Türkiye Cumhuriyeti), is a bi-continental country: an oft-repeated cliché about Turkey is that it is the bridge between Europe and Asia. This is true not only geographically, but also culturally, and many Turks value their European and Asian identities equally.

other.d: the impressive ruins of the medieval Armenian capital, known as the city of a thousand churches

x.around: The site is open daily 08:00-17:00. The entrance fee in 2025 is €8: make sure to ask for a ticket, otherwise your money will be quietly trousered.
x.intro: Ani is an abandoned city in Eastern Anatolia, 44 km east of Kars and right on the border with Armenia. It was the chief city of Armenia in the 11th century, but dwindled thereafter, and was abandoned in the 13th century. Its secular buildings have disappeared and what remains are the stout northern walls and an enclosure dotted with the haunting ruins of religious buildings. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site and ranks among eastern Turkey's top sights.

other.d: an area in the central highlands best known for its unique moon-like landscape (the "fairy chimneys"), underground cities, cave churches and houses carved in the rocks

x.around: The villages are all linked by dolmuş, and these are sufficiently frequent to use for sightseeing.
x.intro: Cappadocia (Turkish: Kapadokya) is an area within South Central Anatolia in Turkey, with a surreal landscape dotted with underground cities, cave churches and houses carved in the rocks.

next.d: is a laid-back city and hub for attractions such as Ihlara Valley or Tuz Gölü the salt lake.
the home of Sufi poet and thinker Rumi has outstanding Seljuk architecture.
is on the route east, and has museums, mosques and a 15th century castle.

other.d: the well-preserved ruins of a Graeco-Roman city on the west coast

x.around: The grounds of Ephesus are seen entirely on foot, and take 90 min to 2.5 hours (plus 30 min for the Terrace Houses). Pathways are signed clearly and easily navigated. The paving of the main avenue is suitable for wheelchairs and strollers, but with lumpy bits and potholes around ongoing works.

hidden.d: Originally at the foot of Arcadiane. Visitors and goods landed and cleared customs here at least until the 2nd century AD.
A puzzle—it contained the body of a 15-18 year old woman but had no inscription. She died circa 50-20 BC, when only the most high-ranking nobles were buried within city walls.
A compulsory photo stop, a splendid marble 48-seater by the Octagon. Only the residents of the Terrace Houses and a handful of other plutocrats had their own sanitary fittings.

This is the only site within Ephesus with an additional admission fee, and it's worth it. This was the upmarket residential quarter, built on the slope above Curetes Street, and blinged with marbles and mosaics.

x.intro: Ephesus (Turkish: Efes) is a with magnificent Roman ruins. It's in the Central Aegean region of Turkey 4 km west of Selçuk and 19 km northeast of the beach resort of Kuşadası.

must.d: It's an attractive compact structure from say 117 AD—that's shortly before Emperor Hadrian busied himself building a wall across northern England, and perhaps the dedication to him came later.

next.d: has the Ephesus Museum, displaying artefacts from the ancient city. Within town is the Byzantine Church of St John, and further out are sights such as the House of the Virgin Mary.
is the raucous beach resort nearby. The Greeks and Romans would have loved it.
might be a three hour drive, as it's north of Izmir, but it's another superb site for the ruins of Pergamon.

other.d: the site of the 1915 Anzac landing and many WWI memorials

x.around: The main highway on the east of the peninsula has buses, but you need a car for the battlefields on the west coast. Otherwise join an organised tour, or negotiate with a taxi driver to take you around for a few hours.
x.intro: Gallipoli redirects here. For other places with the same name, see Gallipoli (disambiguation).

must.d: Impressive citadel built by Fatih Sultan Mehmet in 1463, along with Çimenlik Castle across the straits in Çanakkale.

next.d: across the straits has a few sights, but it's mainly a stopover and transport hub on the route south to Troy and the island of Bozcaada.
island is reached by ferry from Kabatepe west of Eceabat.
of course is not the Gallipoli of 1915 - the attack never got that far - but it's the base for sights in the middle section of the peninsula.

other.d: a UNESCO World Heritage site with ancient statues on its summit, affording a great panorama of its rugged surroundings

x.around: You need your own vehicle to reach the summit of Mount Nemrut, otherwise join an organised tour. Your accommodation will be keen to sell you a tour and will tell fat fibs about why you can't make it solo.
x.intro: Mount Nemrut - the one with giant heads - is described here. The one with a crater lake is near Tatvan. Kâhta is a town in Southeastern Anatolia, with a population of 132,000 in 2023. The reason to visit is Mount Nemrut, only accessible in summer.

next.d: is south towards the Syrian border, and feels Middle Eastern, not least for the automatic weapons on display in the bazaar.
to the north has a museum and several old mosques.
away east if you're collecting mountains called Nemrut: this dormant volcano has a crater lake but no giant heads. Its eruptions blocked the valley outflow to create the hypersaline Lake Van.

other.d: the incomparable postcard beauty of the "Blue Lagoon", perhaps the most iconic beach of Turkey

x.around: Dolmuş minibuses from Fethiye run through Ovacık, Ölüdeniz main village, Hisarönü, and Belceğiz beachfront at the start of Blue Lagoon peninsula.
x.intro: Ölüdeniz is a beach resort in Lycia on the Mediterranean coast of Turkey, famous for its “Blue Lagoon”. It was a tiny place until the 1990s, then Turkish tourism was boosted by direct flights from Europe, and the upgrade of Dalaman Airport put this stretch of coast within a one-hour coach transfer. It was relentlessly marketed, and the Ölüdeniz (Dead Sea) of the flat calm lagoon was re-branded as “blue lagoon”, and came to mean the entire resort strip.

next.d: has Lycian rock tombs gazing down upon the town.
is a ghost village. Its Greek population was deported in 1923, and unlike others it was not re-settled by Turks deported from Greek territory.
to the south is at the foot of Butterfly Valley, a scenic canyon. Kabak is further south, but its canyon is easier to access.

other.d: "the Cotton Castle", a white world of travertines cascading down in a series of shallow pools filled with thermal waters

x.around: Walk: the main sights are within 15 minutes. From the bus stop walk east along Atatürk Cd and cross the main road for the path to Town Gate entrance to the travertines.

hidden.d: This is within the Roman bath house, and displays artifacts found during local excavations, including ornate sarcophagi.

x.intro: Pamukkale is a village in the Southern Aegean region of Turkey, famous for its hot springs, Roman spa town of Hierapolis, and white terraced pools: the village name means "cotton castle". It is a and one of the country's top sights, mobbed in summer. The nearest town is Denizli, 20 km south.

next.d: the nearby transport hub is modern but has several old mosques.
is one of the best preserved Roman sites in this region. It's 30 km west across the mountains, but reckon 50 km winding around by road.
is a big resort town on the Aegean coast. It's close to the ruins of must-see Ephesus; also impressive are the ruins of ancient Didyma, Miletus and Priene.

other.d: a stunning monastery clinging on cliffs; a must-see on any trip to the northeast

x.around: "Take my camel, dear", said my Aunt Dot, as she climbed down from this animal on her return from High Mass. ::: - The Towers of Trebizond (1956) by Rose Macaulay follows a group of conflicted dingbats on a journey from Istanbul

hidden.d: Restored mansion with photographs, documents and artefacts describing the city in the Ottoman and Republican periods. Signage is only in Turkish.
Built in 1987 in retro style on the site of an earlier mosque.
Ottoman mosque built in 1789 around a pre-existing church.
Built in its present form in 1577, this is no longer in use, replaced by a larger modern mosque adjacent.
Majoring on space and aerospace, with planetarium. M-F it may be booked out to school groups.
Art space and cultural centre in the former city governor's mansion.
Former Greek Orthodox church founded in 1306 outside the city walls - exoteichos- but rebuilt in 1856 very much hemmed in by the city. It's now used as an annex to a primary school.

Founded in 1514 by Selim, then governor and later Sultan, in honour of his mother. Gulbahar Hatun (1453-1505) was originally a slave girl and became the concubine of Bayezid II; her tomb is here. The mosque was repaired in 1883.

x.intro: Trabzon is the largest city in the Eastern Karadeniz region of Turkey, with a population of 323,000 in 2023, and another 500,000 in the outlying towns. It was once known as Trebizond, ruling an independent "Empire" around the eastern Black Sea. It's now a lively place with good visitor facilities and attractions.

must.d: A spectacular monastery hewn into a cliff. It was founded in the fourth century, with its heyday in Byzantine and early Ottoman times. It's been ruined and rebuilt several times, but fell derelict after its Greeks were deported.

The city's top sight, a Byzantine church built in the 1250s, with beautiful frescoes, arches and friezes. It became a mosque in 2013 whereupon pre-Islamic features were covered up, but most of these were uncovered in 2020.

The "Golden domed church of All Saints" was built in the 10th or 11th century on much earlier foundations - until the 4th century AD it was the scene of Mithras worship.In the Middle ages it was the city cathedral, and hosted…
Built in the 13th century as a church dedicated to Saint Eugenius, the patron saint of the city. Eugenius was a martyr under the persecutions of Diocletian around 305 AD.

Dinky little Greek Orthodox basilica from 6th / 7th century AD, one of the oldest buildings in the city. It fell out of use when the Greeks were deported and many frescos were painted over, but in 2021 / 22 it was all restored.
Founded in 752 AD, Saint George Peristereota Monastery is now just a few walls teetering on a crag, with cliffs and other pitfalls around: don't come in the fog and drizzle.
The Armenian Monastery of the All-Saviour is on a hill southeast of town. Its foundation date was maybe 1424 AD, over an earlier Greek church.

Founded in 270 AD as one of the first-ever Christian monasteries, now ruined and unsafe. Take the road off D885 towards Köprüyanı, then the track branching uphill from the first hairpin bend - this is only suitable for…

next.d: is a small resort 18 km west.
west is a lively coast resort.
east has a few tourist attractions, but is mostly a stopover heading into the mountains or into Georgia.
is the first place you reach in Georgia. Trabzonites regard it as Las Vegas-on-Sea.
is a mountain resort above Trabzon.
south across Zigana Pass is a base for walking in the hills.
is the next city beyond the mountains.

x.safe: In the city beware traffic, safeguard valuables and avoid lowlife, same as anywhere else.

other.d: a national park featuring school textbook belts of different types of forests varying with altitude, and the major winter sports resort of the country

x.around: There are 2 gondola lifts, 9 chairlifts and 13 T-bar tows. The most extensive ski area is south of the new hotel area and Volfram, on the north-facing slope of the main ridge. You can connect from there to the Fatin Tepe area above the old hotel district. Across the valley from there lies a smaller area.
x.intro: Uludağ (pronounced oo loo daa) is a mountain of 2543 m (8343 ft) elevation which gives its name to a national park and ski resort. It rises just south of Bursa in the Southern Marmara Region of Turkey. The summit ridge is 150 km south of Istanbul, and can be seen from there on very crisp, clear days, but is usually hidden by mist and haze.
